Contributing to sceptre

Source: CONTRIBUTING.md

Contributions to sceptre are welcome, including code, tests, and documentation.

Participation in the project is subject to the Code of Conduct. Please do not include private data, credentials, protected health information, or other sensitive information in pull requests, examples, or test fixtures.

For bug reports, feature requests, and questions about using sceptre, see Getting help with sceptre.

Understand the internals

Start with the objects and how they interact, then trace one analysis before reading the detailed contracts:

  1. Explore the object and workflow map.
  2. Follow one discovery analysis.
  3. Find the right place for a change.
  4. Look up exact object fields, schema contracts, and legacy field decisions as needed.

Import populates ScreenData. Scientific choices belong to AnalysisSpec; compiled design, assignments, and QC to PreparationRecord; compact reusable fits to FitCache; completed output and provenance to ResultRecord. RunPlan and CellView are temporary execution values. Calibration, power, and discovery are sibling analyses after preparation.

The policies and submission checklist below apply to these contributions. Site sources and review status explain how the supporting pages are maintained and what remains to verify.

Contributing code and documentation

Small bug fixes and documentation corrections may be submitted as pull requests without prior discussion.

Before implementing a substantial feature, public API change, or change to statistical methodology, start a feature-request discussion. Early discussion helps the maintainers assess scope, compatibility, and validation requirements before substantial work is invested. Maintainers may promote a sufficiently scoped proposal to an issue for implementation tracking.

Code, tests, and documentation

For the code’s main parts, cell numbering, numerical calculations and pipeline compatibility, see Internal architecture.

Material Where it belongs How long it stays
Package implementation, help, examples and datasets R/, src/, man/, vignettes/, data/, inst/ Permanent; maintain with the package
Tests of current behavior and bug fixes tests/testthat/ Permanent, including regression tests first added during the refactor
CI and current-source C++ checks .github/workflows/, tools/checks/, air.toml Permanent maintainer tooling
Test-input recipes and provenance tools/fixtures/, tests/testthat/fixtures/README.md Permanent; never regenerate expected scientific outputs in CI
Module-map drawing and editable source tools/architecture/ Permanent; maintain with ARCHITECTURE.md
Current architecture and contributor/project guidance Root ARCHITECTURE.md, this guide, README, ROADMAP.md, GOVERNANCE.md and other project policies Permanent; keep current
Refactor tour, manual comparison and validation receipt tools/refactor/; its published archive retains the specification, plans and bulk evidence Temporary; retain for maintainer review, then archive before retiring

Build exclusion does not mean temporary. .Rbuildignore keeps maintainer material out of the distributed R source package. Permanent tools/checks/, tools/fixtures/ and tools/architecture/, and temporary tools/refactor/, are excluded, as are several lasting root guides.

Routine CI uses current-package tests and current-source checks. It must not depend on tools/refactor/, an old SCEPTRE installation or historical comparison outputs. Some permanent tests still have refactor in their filenames; that records their origin, not a plan to delete them. Remove temporary review links when retiring the refactor directory, and keep the lasting architecture guide independent of it.

  • Keep changes focused on a single problem or feature.
  • Add or update tests for behavior changes and bug fixes.
  • Format handwritten R code with Air as described below.
  • Update user-facing documentation when public behavior changes.

Changes affecting model fitting, calibration, power, numerical results, or other statistical behavior generally require more than unit tests. Describe the relevant simulation, benchmark, or reproducible analysis in the pull request.

Formatting R code

Use Air 0.9.0 as the single R formatter. The repository’s air.toml specifies four-space indentation and a preferred width of 80 characters. Format only the handwritten package source, then check it with the same command used by CI:

air format R
air format --check R

Keep Air’s default exclusions for generated bindings. Immutable fixtures and tools/ (including reference code and retained results) are explicitly excluded; do not recursively format tests or reference/evidence directories.

Air does not guarantee that every line is at most 80 characters. Wrap ordinary prose comments and documentation separately where useful, preserving code examples, fenced blocks, URLs, mathematical notation and executable strings. BiocCheck remains a separate Bioconductor checker; Air does not replace its checks or guarantee that every style note is resolved.

Before submitting a pull request

Before submitting a pull request, run a package check:

devtools::check()

Open the pull request against main and explain:

  • the problem being addressed;
  • the proposed change;
  • the tests and checks performed;
  • relevant documentation changes; and
  • any statistical, compatibility, or performance implications.

A maintainer will review the contribution and may request revisions, additional tests, or further validation before merging. Maintainers may decline changes that fall outside the project’s scope or current roadmap.
